audit: The contractor analogy explains distributed ownership, but an abstract task lifecycle can hide which identifier survives a question and which recovery guarantee belongs to an adapter. Lesson A follows incident INC-77 through one input-required pause, preserving the same remote task while the commander supplies a scoped cluster identifier. Lesson B contrasts recovery after a lost creation response with and without an agreed remote deduplication contract. Its unresolved branch stops instead of silently creating a replacement. The examples preserve the distinction between A2A collaboration and MCP capability access, avoid equating duration with protocol choice, and treat received artifacts as evidence requiring acceptance.

lessons.title: A question does not create a second investigation
lessons.intro: The database worker accepts incident INC-77 as task T-904, then needs a cluster identifier. The commander owns the incident throughout this delegated investigation.

data.wait_label: Wait for an authorized cluster ID
data.result: One task continues; artifact acceptance remains pending.

read: Follow T-904 across the pause and continuation.
The saved task survives the missing-information wait.
The commander remains responsible for the incident and final decision.
lessons.question: Should the commander submit a new diagnosis task when the cluster becomes known?
lessons.answer: No. It should answer within scope and continue T-904. Input-required is a pause in this existing task, not evidence that the investigation failed or needs replacement.
lessons.takeaway: Continue the owned task when supplying missing input.
lessons.assumption: Fictional events; authenticated messages and durable storage are assumed. A2A work ownership does not depend on task duration.

lessons.anchor: Timeouts, partial failure and idempotent delegation
lessons.title: Recovering a lost task-creation response
lessons.intro: Both callers persisted delegation D-77. The worker accepted the job, but its creation response was lost before either caller learned the remote task ID.

data.input: D-77 exists locally; remote creation response is missing.

left.title: Agreed remote dedupe
steps: Contract retains D-77 mappings for 24 hours
Retry same key and identical brief at 5 min
Atomic mapping returns original task T-904
left.result: Bind D-77 to T-904; continue the existing investigation

right.title: No dedupe contract
steps: Same message ID has no promised dedupe
Reconcile with the owner before resubmission
right.result: Wait for task identification; do not create replacement work

read: Both callers saved the same local logical identity.
Only the left service promises atomic remote deduplication.
The right caller preserves uncertainty instead of guessing that creation failed.
lessons.question: Can the right caller obtain the left outcome merely by reusing its message ID?
lessons.answer: No. A stable message ID alone does not require A2A Send Message deduplication. The service must implement and document the key scope, retention, same-payload checks and recovery path.
lessons.takeaway: A local key needs a remote recovery contract.
lessons.assumption: Fictional adapter extension; the left retry occurs inside its retention window. A2A itself does not require this behavior.
